evidence_quotes.quote: Compliance with the SDWA does not equate with safe drinking water quality, so this study cannot be considered an environmental justice analysis of access to safe drinking water.
3) Are there additional characteristics of the CWS such as size of the water system, public versus private ownership, and water source parameters that influence compliance with the SDWA?
A negative binomial regression model was used to determine which characteristics of the water system and population served by the water system best predicted the number of violations.
These data were processed to produce a dataset that includes the number of total violations and number of health-based violations within the time period of interest.

Health-based violations consist of exceedances of MCLs, exceedances of disinfectant concentration thresholds, and improper water treatment (U.S. EPA, 2017c). Non-health-based violations include failure to monitor regularly or report results on-time, failure to notify the public that there is a serious health problem with drinking water, and failure to publish annual consumer confidence reports (U.S. EPA, 2017c).

criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access. All observations are already-active community water systems (inactive systems and areas served by private wells are excluded), and the study examines regulatory drinking-water quality and administrative monitoring/reporting violations rather than access to water services.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this would be 'yes' because the paper examines regulatory compliance with the federal Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) and includes public versus private utility ownership (and wholesale purchased water) as institutional predictors. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, however, it is 'no' because Criterion 2 requires a rule-type mechanism (including enforcement or utility ownership/regulatory structure) directly governing service access, whereas here utility ownership and SDWA regulation are analyzed solely as determinants of contaminant/treatment and monitoring/reporting violations at active utilities, not rules or structures governing household or community service access, connection, pricing, or disconnection.
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical spatial and econometric analysis of 1,694 active CWSs in Pennsylvania (2012-2016) combining PA DEP CWS boundary GIS data, EPA SDWIS violation records, U.S. Census/ACS sociodemographic data, and USGS NLCD land cover data, estimated via negative binomial regression.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports only five-year counts of total SDWA violations and health-based SDWA violations (MCL exceedances, disinfectant/treatment technique violations, and monitoring, reporting, and public-notification violations). Does not measure service access, connection, service availability, reliability/continuity, quantity, affordability, disconnection, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (1,694 active CWSs in Pennsylvania), exposures/covariates (poverty rate, racial/ethnic composition across four spatial methods, rurality, public vs. private ownership, purchased water, system size <200 connections, groundwater source), outcomes (total and health-based SDWA violation counts, 2012-2016), and cross-sectional spatial/negative binomial regression design are clearly specified.

study_design: Cross-sectional spatial and econometric observational study (comparing areal weighting, dasymetric mapping, areal interpolation, and county-level aggregation with negative binomial regression)
population_and_sample: Active community water systems (CWSs) in Pennsylvania: 1,694 active CWSs analyzed across four spatial estimation methods (from 1,833 active CWS boundaries in the PA DEP shapefile, linked to 3,166 census tracts and 67 counties)
exposure: Estimated CWS service-area sociodemographics (% below poverty line, % people of color / non-Hispanic white across four spatial estimation methods) and CWS characteristics: public vs. private ownership, rural vs. urban classification, system size (<200 vs. >200 connections), purchased vs. unpurchased water, and groundwater vs. surface water source
outcome: Counts of total Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) violations and health-based SDWA violations per active community water system from January 1, 2012 to December 31, 2016
rationale: Excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome). Although this empirical spatial-econometric study examines community water systems in Pennsylvania and includes public versus private utility ownership alongside sociodemographic and technical system characteristics, its sole outcomes are utility-level counts of total and health-based Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) water-quality and monitoring/reporting violations among already-active water systems. It does not measure household or community water service access, connection, availability, reliability/continuity, water quantity, affordability, utility-account eligibility, disconnection, or exclusion (failing c1 and c4, and consequently failing the narrow 2026-10-13 c2 requirement that the legal/institutional mechanism govern service access). Statistical significance or direction of the reported estimates played no role in this decision.
